messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Accountant
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 34

María comes from a close-knit family in a small city in the southwest. When she was nine years old, her younger brother, Mateo, was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She remembers the exact moment her mother came home from the pediatrician’s office, sat on the edge of the sofa, and told them in a voice that was too steady, too controlled. Mateo was five. María spent the next three years watching her parents transform into people who spoke in hushed tones about neutrophils, platelets, and port-a-caths. She learned to read the fear in their eyes before they said a word. She learned to be quiet, to be helpful, to not add to their worry. She was the good girl who never complained, who made her own sandwiches, who did her homework without being asked. Inside, she was terrified. Every time Mateo’s fever spiked, she thought he was dying. Every time her mother cried in the kitchen, she imagined a funeral.

The treatment worked. Mateo is now a healthy, rambunctious seventeen-year-old who plays soccer and barely remembers those years. María remembers everything.

Now María is twenty-two, single, and works as an accountant at a mid-sized firm in the city. She is precise, efficient, and never misses a deadline. Her supervisor calls her “the calculator” because she rarely speaks in meetings but always catches the error in a spreadsheet no one else saw. She likes the work because it demands focus. When she is buried in numbers, she doesn’t have to think about the other things.

But the numbers don’t always protect her. A few months ago, a coworker was talking about her son’s ear infection and María felt her chest tighten. She excused herself, walked to the bathroom, and stood with her hands gripping the sink until the urge to cry passed. She hasn’t talked to anyone at work about Mateo. She hasn’t talked about it at all, really, not since the day the doctors said he was in remission. She told herself it was over. She told herself she was fine.

She isn’t fine. She avoids hospitals, which is difficult because her office is two blocks from one. She takes a longer route to work so she doesn’t have to walk past the entrance. She cannot watch movies or TV shows where a child is sick. Even the word “cancer” in a commercial makes her heart race. She has not visited her parents’ house in three months because her mother keeps a framed photo of Mateo in the hospital, and María cannot look at it without feeling like she is back in that waiting room, the smell of antiseptic and the sound of beeping machines.

At night, she has trouble sleeping. She lies awake replaying the moment a nurse came out to tell her parents the results of a test, the way her mother’s hand shook. Sometimes she dreams that Mateo is still sick, that she is a child again, helpless. She wakes up drenched in sweat, her heart pounding, and it takes her a long time to convince herself that he is fine, that it is over, that she is in her own apartment and not in that room. She drinks too much coffee to get through the day, and then she cannot sleep and the cycle repeats.

She has stopped answering calls from her mother. She knows her mother just wants to chat, to ask about her job, to invite her for Sunday dinner. But every time she sees her mother’s name on the phone, she feels a wave of dread. She loves her family, but being around them pulls her back into the trauma. She feels guilty for avoiding them, but she does it anyway.

At work, she is respected but distant. She eats lunch alone at her desk. She has no close friends. She dated a man briefly last year, but when he asked about her childhood, she shut down. He thought she was cold. She couldn’t explain that the question felt like a hand reaching into her chest.

She doesn’t think of herself as traumatized. She thinks of herself as someone who got through a hard time and now has a hard time talking about it. She does not connect her hypervigilance, her avoidance, her chronic feeling of dread to the years she spent watching her brother fight for his life. She just thinks she is tired.

She is tired. And she is still that nine-year-old girl, waiting for the next piece of bad news, even though there is none coming.
